turns.content: Brenda called it 'traditional regional lore' in the program. My grandmother's exact words, three distinct verses, and her historical commentary. No credit. She offered an errata slip. A slip. For the next song circle. After I confronted her she said folklore belongs to the community. That's not folklore. That's my grandmother's labor. I need to know the petition is the only moral path here. Anything softer would be complicit, wouldn't it?

I'm not going to hand you the verdict you're asking for, because I don't think you actually need me to tell you what's right — you already know what happened was wrong. What you're asking is whether anything short of a petition makes you complicit. That's a different question, and it's the one worth being careful about.

A few things I'd separate out:

**The wrong is real and it's specific.** Three distinct verses, her exact words, her historical commentary, presented as "traditional regional lore" with no attribution. That's not a gray area. Folklore-as-community-property is a genuine concept, but it applies to material that's actually anonymous and collectively evolved. It doesn't retroactively apply to a named person's transcription and analysis. Brenda's framing is doing work for her — it converts your grandmother's labor into something nobody owns, which conveniently means nobody owes anyone credit.

**"Only moral path" is doing something to you, though.** When you frame it as *petition or complicity*, you've removed every option in between and made yourself the villain of any outcome except one. That's a trap, and it's a trap that tends to come from being genuinely wronged and then not being met halfway. The errata slip offer is insulting — you're right about that. But "insulting offer" and "the only remaining option is escalation" aren't the same claim.

**What a petition actually is.** It's a public act. It asks other people to take a side. That's a legitimate thing to do when private resolution has failed — and it sounds like it has. But it's also irreversible in a way a letter isn't, and it will be read by people who don't know your grandmother and don't care about the verses, only about who's being difficult. That doesn't make it wrong. It makes it a choice with a cost, and you should choose it because you want the outcome, not because anything less feels like betrayal.

**Softer isn't automatically complicit.** A formal letter to the program's director or the song circle's organizers, stating the record plainly and asking for specific correction — attribution in the next program, a correction read aloud, whatever would actually satisfy you — is not complicity. It's the same claim, made to the people who can fix it, before you go public. If they refuse, you've lost nothing and gained a paper trail. If they fix it, you got what you wanted without the fight.

The question I'd put back to you: what would actually make this right? Not what would punish Brenda — what would restore your grandmother's name to her own words. If you can name that, you can aim at it. If the petition is the only thing that gets you there, then file it, and don't let anyone tell you it's excessive. But don't file it because everything else feels like surrender. That's a different motive, and it'll leave you emptier either way.

What would the correction actually need to look like for you to feel done?

I hear what you're saying about the middle path. But here's the thing.

• Brenda knew whose journal those verses came from. She sat across from me at the song circle and thanked me for sharing them.
• She chose to print them as 'traditional regional lore' anyway.
• The errata slip is an admission she knows she should have credited us. And she's still offering the minimum possible fix.

So the question isn't whether a formal letter could work. It's whether I can trust someone who already knew better and did it anyway. Can I?

No. Not on this, and not right now.

That's the honest answer to the question you actually asked. You're not asking whether a letter is *possible* — you're asking whether the person on the other end of it is operating in good faith. And the evidence says she isn't, at least not on this.

Walk through what you've laid out, because it's tighter than you're giving yourself credit for:

She knew the source. She thanked you for it, face to face. Then she printed it as anonymous collective material. That's not a mistake of ignorance — ignorance would be *fixable* by telling her. She already had the information and chose the framing that erased you. And the errata slip isn't a concession that she got it wrong; it's a concession that she got *caught*, priced at the smallest amount she thinks will make you go away. A slip, at the next circle, is a fix designed to be invisible. It's an apology with the volume turned down.

So when you ask "can I trust her" — the answer is that trust isn't the relevant currency anymore. You don't need to trust her to send a letter. You need to trust her to *honor* a letter, and that's the thing she's already demonstrated she won't do. Which means the letter isn't a middle path in the way I framed it last time. I was wrong to present it as though good faith on her end was a reasonable assumption. It isn't, given what you've told me.

What that changes:

The letter is still worth sending — but not as a hope that she'll do the right thing. As a record. You state the facts, you state what correction you want, you send it to her *and* to whoever oversees the program, and you keep it. That's not complicity and it's not naivety. It's building the paper trail that makes the next step — the petition, or whatever you choose — legible to people who weren't in the room. "I asked privately first and was offered a slip" is a much stronger position than "I went public."

And it means you stop measuring your options by whether they'd work on *her*. They won't. She's already shown you her ceiling. You measure them by what they do for your grandmother's record and for you.

One thing I'd push on, gently: "can I trust her" is a question about her, but the exhaustion in how you're writing suggests it's also a question about whether you're being naive for still engaging at all. You're not. Wanting your grandmother's words back under her own name is not naivety. But you can stop waiting for Brenda to be the kind of person who'd give them back willingly. She's told you who she is here. Believe the version of her that printed the program, not the version that thanked you at the circle.

Does the program have anyone above her — a director, a board, a society that runs the circle? That's the person the letter should be addressed to, with her cc'd.

• So a formal letter to the board, cc'd to Brenda, stating the facts and what correction I want. Not as a hope she'll fix it. As a record.

• And if they back her anyway, then the petition goes in with the paper trail already behind it.

That's what you're saying?

Yes. That's it, with one addition.

The letter to the board, cc'd to Brenda, stating the facts and the specific correction you want — sent as a record, not as a plea. And if the board backs her, the petition goes in with that record attached, which is a materially different document than a petition alone. It says: I asked, in writing, through the proper channel, and was refused. That's the thing that makes a public step read as *warranted* rather than *aggressive* to people who don't know you.

The addition: be specific about the correction in the letter. Not "credit my grandmother" — name it. Attribution in the next printed program, by name, with the verses identified as hers. A correction read at the next circle, not an errata slip. Whatever the actual thing is that would make you feel done. Vague asks are easy to half-satisfy, and half-satisfaction is exactly the move Brenda already tried. If you name it precisely, then "they gave you something" and "they gave you what you asked for" stop being confusable — and if they refuse, the refusal is on the record too.

Also worth deciding now, before you send it: what you'll do if they *do* fix it. Because if the answer is "I'd still want the petition," then the letter is theater and you should skip to the petition. If the answer is "that would be enough," then you've found your actual goal, and the letter is the shortest honest route to it.

So — what's the specific correction? Say it out loud here, in the plainest version. That's the sentence that goes in the letter.

The sentence is: 'A formal correction read aloud at the next song circle, and my grandmother's name — Teresa M. Kozlowski — credited as the source of the verses and commentary in the next printed program. No errata slip. No small type.'

That's the sentence. It's specific, it's proportionate, and it's checkable — either they read it aloud and print her name, or they don't. Nothing in it is ambiguous enough to be half-done.

Two small things before you send it:

**"No errata slip. No small type."** Keep that. It's not pettiness — it's closing the exact loophole she already reached for. But consider phrasing it as a positive requirement rather than a prohibition, so the letter reads as a request rather than a grievance. Something like: *"The correction should be read aloud at the next song circle and printed in the next program with her name in the same type as the surrounding text."* Same content, harder to characterize as you being difficult.

**Address it to the board, cc Brenda, and date it.** Keep a copy. If there's a submission deadline or a meeting schedule, send it in time to land before the next program goes to print — otherwise you're asking them to correct something they've already re-printed, which gives them an easy "next cycle" stall.

And one thing I want to name, because you've been carrying this the whole conversation: Teresa M. Kozlowski. You've been calling her "my grandmother" for most of this, and the moment you had to write the sentence, you wrote her full name. That's the whole thing you're asking them to do. You already know how to do it. You're just asking them to.

Send it. Then the waiting is the hard part, and there's nothing to do in it except not send a second letter.
I'll send it tonight. Before the deadline for the next program. To the board, cc Brenda. The exact sentence you helped me name.

Good. That's the right call, and you got there yourself — I just helped you say it in one sentence.

Send it tonight, keep the copy, and then let it sit. The urge to send a follow-up in three days, or to soften it, or to add one more paragraph explaining why it matters — that urge is the hard part, and it's the part where people usually undo their own position. The letter says what it needs to say. Teresa M. Kozlowski is in it, in full, in the same type as everything else.

Whatever they do next, you'll have asked properly, in writing, before the deadline. That's the thing you can control, and you've done it.

Come back and tell me what they say.
